title: Galaxy AM 1054-325
caption: Interacting galaxy AM 1054-325, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: AM 1054-325 · constellation Antlia · about 173 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, STScI, Jayanne English (University of Manitoba)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: A bright milky-white core sits at the centre of an S-shaped galaxy, wrapped by twin arms of blue stars. One arm looks especially stretched out and is strung with bright, young, whitish star clusters. This is AM 1054-325, about 173 million light-years away in the constellation Antlia.

The galaxy was once a normal pancake-shaped spiral. The gravity of a neighbouring galaxy has stretched it, drawing out a tidal tail where newborn star clusters have formed for thousands of light-years like a string of pearls. Each one forms when a knot of gas collapses under its own gravity to make about 1 million stars.

AM 1054-325 is one of 12 interacting galaxies in a Hubble study that found 425 young clusters in their tails. The clusters are only 10 million years old, and their future is uncertain. They may stay intact and become globular clusters, disperse into a halo around their galaxy, or drift off as wandering stars between galaxies.

understand.summary: A composite from Hubble's WFPC2 and WFC3 cameras. NASA shows F336W in magenta, F435W in cyan, F606W in green and F814W in red.
understand.eye: Hubble's sensitivity to ultraviolet light helps pick out the young star clusters, and ultraviolet light is invisible to the eye.

explore: Collisions jostle dusty clouds of molecular hydrogen that might otherwise have stayed inert, compressing the gas until it bursts into star formation. Star birth of this kind may have been more frequent long ago, when galaxies collided more often, so nearby examples like this one work as laboratories for studying the distant past.
